reasoning: The core problem — whether a model's self-evaluation misses overlap with its own generation errors, and how this compares to a different-model grader — is well covered by multiple recent published works. "Self-Correction Bench" (arXiv 2507.02778, NeurIPS 2025) names and measures the "Self-Correction Blind Spot": non-reasoning LLMs fail on 64.5% of errors in their own outputs while correcting identical external errors, isolating the self vs. external attribution effect that this proposal targets. "Self-Attribution Bias: When AI Monitors Go Easy on Themselves" (arXiv 2603.04582) shows self-attribution bias is largest precisely on incorrect outputs and harmful actions, matching the proposal's safety-oversight framing. Crucially, the proposed methodological control (a different-family model of similar size as a baseline for generic judging difficulty) is essentially the "proxy model of similar capability / Evaluator Quality Baseline" already used in self-preference work ("Are LLM Evaluators Really Narcissists?", arXiv 2601.22548) and in self-evaluation TPR/TNR studies reporting models endorse 95%+ of their own errors. The remaining gap is minor: the exact restriction to items the model answered wrong, plus a clean same-size cross-family control on those items, is a specific framing not pinned to a single paper, but the contribution it would yield is largely subsumed by existing results.

evidence.title: Self-Correction Bench: Uncovering and Addressing the Self-Correction Blind Spot in Large Language Models
evidence.summary: Introduces the 'Self-Correction Blind Spot': across 14 open non-reasoning models, models fail to correct 64.5% of errors in their OWN outputs while successfully correcting identical errors from external sources. Directly establishes that attribution (self vs external) modulates error detection — the exact gap this proposal aims to measure.

evidence.title: Self-Attribution Bias: When AI Monitors Go Easy on Themselves
evidence.summary: Finds self-attribution bias is largest on incorrect code and harmful actions — precisely where reliable self-monitoring matters. Frames the phenomenon as a safety/oversight concern (judges sharing the policy model's blind spot give no corrective signal), matching the proposal's motivation.

evidence.title: Are LLM Evaluators Really Narcissists? Sanity Checking Self-Preference Evaluations
evidence.summary: Measures self-preference per-example by comparing how much a judge prefers its own incorrect response vs that of a proxy model of similar capability ('Evaluator Quality Baseline') — essentially the proposed same-size cross-grader control for isolating the self-evaluation blind spot from generic judging difficulty.

evidence.title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
evidence.summary: Establishes self-recognition is linearly correlated with self-preference, the foundational mechanism for a model failing to penalize its own errors. Underpins the proposal's hypothesis about self-endorsement of own wrong answers.

evidence.title: The Generative AI Paradox on Evaluation: What It Can Solve, It May Not Evaluate (and related self-evaluation TPR/TNR studies)
evidence.summary: Self-evaluation TPR/TNR analyses report models endorsing 95%+ of their own errors (e.g., very low true-negative rates on self-grading wrong answers) and that cross-family verifiers outperform self-verification on math/logic — quantifying the self-endorsement-of-wrong-answers rate the proposal would re-measure.
